title: Research Skills for Students
summary: Learn to choose a topic, ask a good research question, find and judge sources, take honest notes, cite correctly and collect data ethically.

lessons.title: Choosing a topic and writing a research question

body.p: Research is a careful search for answers to a question. Every good research project starts by choosing a topic that is interesting, possible to finish in the time you have, and narrow enough to handle. A topic like 'Education' is far too wide: whole libraries have been written about it. A topic like 'How does sleep affect concentration in Year 10 students at my school?' is much more manageable.

steps: Start with a broad area you care about, for example 'Technology and school'.
Ask: which part? Phones, online learning, computer rooms, or calculators?
Narrow by group: which students, which age or class?
Narrow by place and time: your school, your town, the last two years.
Check that you can find information on it and complete it in the time given.

body.p: Example: Technology and school becomes phones in class, then phone use during revision by senior students, then 'How does phone use during evening revision affect the quality of revision among Year 11 students?'

body.h: Turning a topic into a research question

body.p: A good research question is clear, focused, answerable with evidence and not answerable with just yes or no. Compare the three questions below.

body.code:
Weak: Are phones bad?
Better: Do phones harm students?
Strong: How does phone use during evening revision affect how much Year 11 students report remembering the next day?

body.p: The first is vague and loaded. The second can be answered by yes or no and uses the vague word 'harm'. The third names the group, the activity and what will be measured. It can be investigated with a short survey and a memory test.

body.tip: Test your question: could two researchers with the same question know what to do first? If not, it needs to be clearer.

body.p: A source is anywhere you get information from. Good researchers use a mix of sources and know what each is for. Start by listing keywords from your question, plus alternative words. For the phone question you might use 'phone', 'mobile', 'smartphone', 'revision', 'study', 'memory' and 'distraction'.

list: Library catalogues: search by title, author or subject to find books. School and university libraries also give access to ebooks. Note the shelf number, such as the classification number, to find the book quickly.

Academic journals: articles written by researchers and checked by other experts before publication (peer review). They are ideal for evidence. Many universities give students free access through the library.

Reliable websites: government and statistics offices, exam boards, universities and well-known international organisations. Look at the address ending and the 'About' page, but remember that an ending alone does not guarantee quality.
Newspapers and magazines: useful for current events and opinion, but check how they know what they say.
People: teachers, librarians and community experts, who can be interviewed.

body.p: A primary source is first-hand evidence: a diary, an interview you do yourself, a survey, an original photograph, a law, or the data itself. A secondary source explains or interprets primary sources: a textbook, a review article or a documentary. If you study the history of your town, a letter written in 1960 is primary; a book about the 1960s written last year is secondary. For most school projects you will use mainly secondary sources and perhaps a small amount of your own primary data.

steps: Use specific phrases in quotation marks, for example "revision habits".
Combine words, for example sleep AND concentration AND adolescents.
Try a different word if you get nothing.
Look at the reference list of a good source to find more.
Ask the librarian: this is part of their job.

body.tip: Wikipedia and general search results are fine for getting ideas and keywords, but do not usually count as a final source for serious work. Follow its references to the originals.

body.p: Not all sources are equally trustworthy. Evaluating a source means deciding how much you can rely on it. A simple checklist is authority, date, evidence and bias.

list: Authority: Who wrote it? What qualifications or experience do they have on this subject? Which organisation published it? A nutritionist writing about diet is more authoritative than a gaming blogger.
Date: When was it published or updated? In fast-changing fields such as technology or medicine, older sources may be out of date. In history, an older source may be fine, even valuable.
Evidence: Does it give data, explain its method and name its sources so you can check? Or does it only make claims?

Bias: Does the author gain from you believing this? A company's page about its own product is likely to show only good points. Bias does not make a source useless, but you must read it with care and compare it with others.

body.p: You want evidence about study habits. Source A is a journal article by two education researchers at a university, published three years ago, describing a survey of students, how they chose the sample and what the limits were. Source B is an anonymous blog post with no date saying, 'Studying with music always works!' and linking to a shop selling headphones. Source C is a teacher's website that gives revision advice from experience.

body.code:
Source A: strong authority, recent, clear evidence, little obvious bias.
Source B: no authority, no date, no evidence, commercial bias.
Source C: some authority from experience, evidence limited, low bias.

body.p: You would rely mainly on A, use C to give a practical example, and leave B out. Even source A should be compared with another study, because one study can be wrong or limited to one group.

body.tip: Ask 'How do they know?' about any claim. If the source cannot answer, be careful.

lessons.title: Taking notes, a source log, and avoiding plagiarism

body.p: Good notes make writing easier and protect you from accidental plagiarism. Plagiarism means presenting someone else's words or ideas as your own. It can lead to lost marks or worse. It is not only copying a whole essay: copying a sentence without credit, or changing a few words and leaving the rest, also counts.

As soon as you use a source, record the details you will need for your reference list. Doing this later, when you have forgotten where things came from, is slow and error-prone. A simple table in your notebook or on your phone will do.

body.code:
No. | Author | Year | Title | Where found / page or URL | Date accessed | Notes
1   | Mensah & Boateng | 2021 | Sleep and exam performance... | Journal of Student Studies 12(3), pp. 45-58 | 5 May 2025 | Survey of students; sleep and marks link
2   | Example Education Board | 2024 | Exam timetable guidance | website URL | 12 May 2025 | Dates and rules

list: Quoting: copying exact words, inside quotation marks, with the author, year and page number. Use sparingly, for striking or technical wording.
Paraphrasing: restating a specific idea fully in your own words and sentence structure, and still citing the source.
Summarising: a short account of the main points of a longer text, in your own words, with a citation.

body.p: Original: 'Students who slept eight hours or more reported higher concentration in morning lessons.' A poor paraphrase, which changes only a few words: 'Students who slept eight hours or more said they had higher concentration in morning classes.' This is too close and still needs quotation marks or rewriting. A good paraphrase after understanding it: 'Longer sleep was linked to students feeling more focused at the start of the school day (Mensah and Boateng, 2021).'

steps: Read a section, then close the book.
Write the main idea in your own words from memory.
Check against the source for accuracy.
Put quotation marks around any exact words, and add the page number.
Add the source number from your log to every note.

body.tip: When in doubt, cite. You can never lose marks for giving credit.

lessons.title: Citing sources and writing a reference list

body.p: Citing tells the reader where your information came from, shows respect for other people's work, and lets your reader check it. Two systems are in common use: Harvard and APA. Both are author-date styles. In the text, you give the author's surname and year in brackets. At the end, a reference list gives the full details in alphabetical order by surname. Always follow the style your school or university asks for. Small differences exist between institutions, so use their guide if it is different from the examples here.

The examples below use invented authors and organisations for practice. In real work, titles of books, journals and websites follow the style's rules for italics. Here they are shown in plain text, so check which parts to italicise in your guide: in Harvard, the book title, journal name and web page title are in italics; in APA, the book title, the journal name and volume number, and the web page title are in italics.

body.code:
Harvard, one author:   (Okafor, 2019)
Harvard, two authors:  (Mensah and Boateng, 2021)
Harvard, with quote:   (Okafor, 2019, p. 14)
APA, one author:       (Okafor, 2019)
APA, two authors:      (Mensah & Boateng, 2021)
APA, with quote:       (Okafor, 2019, p. 14)

Harvard:
Okafor, N. (2019) Learning to research. Lagos: Example Press.

APA:
Okafor, N. (2019). Learning to research. Example Press.

Harvard:
Mensah, K. and Boateng, A. (2021) 'Sleep and exam performance in secondary students', Journal of Student Studies, 12(3), pp. 45-58.

APA:
Mensah, K., & Boateng, A. (2021). Sleep and exam performance in secondary students. Journal of Student Studies, 12(3), 45-58.

body.p: If the article has a DOI (a permanent web address), add it at the end. In APA write it as a link, such as https://doi.org/..., after the page numbers. Notice the differences: Harvard uses 'and' and APA uses '&' between authors; Harvard puts the article title in single quotation marks, while APA does not; Harvard writes 'pp.' before page numbers, while APA does not. APA also includes a full stop after the year in brackets, and the publisher's place is not given for books.

body.code:
Harvard:
Example Education Board (2024) Exam timetable guidance. Available at: https://www.example.org/guidance (Accessed: 12 May 2025).

APA:
Example Education Board. (2024, March 8). Exam timetable guidance. https://www.example.org/guidance

body.p: Harvard needs the date you accessed the page. APA usually does not, unless the page is likely to change. If a web page has no date, write (n.d.) in both styles. Put the list in alphabetical order: Example, then Mensah, then Okafor.

body.tip: Build your reference list as you go, from your source log, and check every in-text citation appears in the list and the other way round.

lessons.title: Surveys, interviews, ethics and organising findings

body.p: Sometimes the answer to your question is not in books and you need to collect your own data. Two simple tools for school projects are surveys and interviews. A survey asks the same short questions to many people and is good for counting. An interview is a conversation with a few people and is good for explanations and detail.

list: Ask one thing at a time. Not 'Do you sleep well and revise daily?'
Avoid leading questions. Not 'Don't you agree phones ruin revision?' but 'How often do you use your phone while revising?'
Give clear answer choices such as 'never', 'sometimes', 'often'.
Keep it short, and test it on two friends first.
Choose a fair sample: not only your friends, but students from different classes.

body.p: Suppose you survey 40 students and 26 say they use their phone during revision. Then 14 do not. As percentages that is 65 percent and 35 percent. You can report it as '26 of 40 students (65 percent) said they use their phone while revising.' Always give both the number and the total, and say how many you asked, since a percent alone can mislead. Do not claim your result proves anything about all students in the country: it describes only the group you asked.

list: Consent: explain the purpose in plain words, say the study is voluntary, and let people say no or stop at any time. For students under 18, follow your school's rules, which usually mean asking a teacher or parent as well.
Anonymity: do not record names unless needed. Report results in a way that nobody can be identified. If you must record names, keep them separate and private.
Confidentiality: do not share what an individual said with others.
No harm: do not ask upsetting or unnecessary personal questions, and do not put anyone under pressure.
Honesty: report your results as they are, even if they do not support what you hoped.

body.p: Once you have collected sources and data, group your notes under headings before writing. Put the answer to your research question at the centre.

body.code:
Title and research question
1. Introduction: why the topic matters, the question
2. What other sources say (literature): themes with citations
3. Method: survey of 40 students, how chosen, ethics
4. Findings: key numbers, quotes from interviews
5. Discussion: what it means, limits of the study
6. Conclusion: the direct answer to the question
Reference list

body.tip: If a note does not fit any heading, either it does not belong in this project or your outline needs a new heading.

quiz.q: Which research question is the strongest for a Year 10 project?
options: How does the number of hours my schoolmates sleep on school nights relate to their morning concentration?
Is sleep good or bad for people, and what do doctors, teachers and parents think about it?
What is everything that has ever been discovered, written or taught about education around the world?
Why are so many students lazy, and what punishments should schools use to make them work harder?

quiz.q: A student wants to research 'Sport'. What is the best first step in narrowing this?
options: Read as many books and articles about sport as possible before deciding what to focus on
Choose a specific sport, group and place, such as netball participation among girls at her school
Pick a completely different subject that feels easier, such as music, and start again from scratch
Widen the topic to all sports in all countries so that there is plenty of material to use

quiz.q: You need a first-hand account of life in your town in the 1960s. Which is a primary source?
options: A textbook chapter on your country's history, written by a historian decades later
A website summarising the town's history, written last year by a local group
A recorded interview with a resident who lived in the town during that decade
A documentary made in 2020 about the decade, using archive footage

quiz.q: You find three web pages on the same health topic. Which is the most credible?
options: An anonymous page with no listed author, no date and no references to any research
A page run by a company that sells a supplement for the condition it describes
A forum post with thousands of likes from people describing their own experiences
A national health ministry page naming its sources and the date it was updated

quiz.q: A company website says its own product is 'the best in the world'. How should you treat it?
options: As a possible biased source, to be compared with independent evidence
As reliable, because the company knows its own product better than anyone
As reliable, because it uses confident language and strong claims
As worthless, so it should be ignored when researching the product

quiz.q: The original text says: 'Reading for twenty minutes a day was linked to better vocabulary scores.' Which is the best paraphrase?
options: Reading for twenty minutes a day was linked to better vocabulary scores.
Short daily reading was associated with stronger vocabulary results (Author, 2020).
Reading for twenty minutes a day was linked to better vocabulary results.
Daily reading for twenty minutes produced better vocabulary scores, as I found in my own tests.

quiz.q: Which of these counts as plagiarism?
options: Quoting a sentence in quotation marks with the author, year and page number
Paraphrasing an idea fully in your own words and citing the source in both the text and the list
Copying two sentences from a website into your essay without quotation marks or a citation
Listing the book in your reference list and citing it in the text where it is used

quiz.q: Which is the correct Harvard reference-list entry for the book (author N. Okafor, 2019, Learning to research, Lagos, Example Press)?
options: Okafor, N. (2019). Learning to research. Example Press.
N. Okafor, Learning to research, 2019, published by Example Press, Lagos.
Learning to research, by Okafor, N. (Lagos, Example Press), 2019.
Okafor, N. (2019) Learning to research. Lagos: Example Press.

quiz.q: Which is the correct APA entry for the journal article by K. Mensah and A. Boateng (2021), 'Sleep and exam performance in secondary students', Journal of Student Studies, volume 12, issue 3, pages 45-58?
options: Mensah, K., & Boateng, A. (2021). Sleep and exam performance in secondary students. Journal of Student Studies, 12(3), 45-58.
Mensah, K. and Boateng, A. (2021) 'Sleep and exam performance in secondary students', Journal of Student Studies, 12(3), pp. 45-58.
Mensah and Boateng (2021) Sleep and exam performance in students, Journal of Student Studies, vol 12, pages 45-58.
Journal of Student Studies (2021). Mensah, K. & Boateng, A.: Sleep and exam performance in secondary students, 12, 3.

quiz.q: In which order should a reference list be arranged?
options: By the order in which you happened to find each source
Alphabetically by the first author's surname
By the number of words in each source's title
By how much you liked or trusted each source

quiz.q: A web page in the Harvard style has no publication date. What goes in the year position?
options: The current year, without any note
The word 'unknown' placed in the title
n.d. (the abbreviation for 'no date')
Leave the whole reference out of the list

quiz.q: Which survey question is least biased?
options: Don't you agree that phones ruin revision for most students these days?
Isn't it true that most sensible students switch off their phones when revising?
Do you waste time on your phone and avoid revising for your exams?
How often do you use your phone while revising: never, sometimes or often?

quiz.q: Out of 40 students surveyed, 26 use their phone during revision. Which statement reports this accurately and cautiously?
options: 26 of 40 students (65 percent) in this survey said they use their phone during revision.
65 percent of all students in the country use their phone during revision, as this survey shows.
The survey proves that phones help revision, since 26 of the 40 students said they use one.
The other 14 students are lying about their phone use, so the results are unreliable.

quiz.q: Before interviewing a classmate for a project, which is the most ethical step?
options: Record the interview secretly so that they act naturally and you capture the most honest answers
Explain the purpose, say taking part is voluntary and ask permission to record or note answers
Promise to publish their full name and answers widely so they feel proud of taking part
Pressure them to take part if they hesitate, since the project deadline is close

quiz.q: Your survey includes sensitive answers. How can you protect participants' anonymity?
options: Write each student's name next to their answer in the final report
Share the completed forms with the class so everyone can discuss them
Do not collect names, and report only combined group results
Leave the completed forms in a public place where people can read them

quiz.q: You have collected sources and data. What should you do next, before writing?
options: Start writing straight away and add the sources later from memory once you finish
Copy the introduction from your best source and change a few words so it reads smoothly
Delete the notes that do not agree with your expected answer to the research question
Group your notes under headings to build an outline that answers the research question
